sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

content.text: Read TASK.md and carry out every step in order.

# Your task (after reading)

You are a student reader helping an editor test a teaching article before it is published.
Work only inside this directory. Do not search the web. Be honest: the editor needs to know
where the article fails to teach.

1. Read `article.md` from start to finish.
2. Answer the questions in its "Check your understanding" section. Write the answers to
   `answers.md`, numbered like the questions. Two to six sentences each, in your own words; show
   working where a question asks for a calculation or a translation. After each answer add a line
   `Confidence: N` with N from 1 (guessing) to 5 (certain).
3. Write `feedback.md` with these sections:
   - **Passages I had to read twice**: quote each (one or two sentences) and say what was unclear.
   - **Terms used before they were explained, or never explained**: one line each.
   - **Claims I could not verify from the article itself**: quote each and say what evidence or
     step is missing.
   - **Section scores**: for each numbered section, a score from 1 (lost) to 5 (clear) and one
     sentence of reason.
   - **Questions that the article did not let me answer**: which quiz questions, if any, could not
     be answered from the text, and what was missing.
   - **One thing to add and one thing to cut**.
4. Write `diary.md`: a work diary of this session in the format of `diary-format.md`, with one
   step for reading, one for the quiz and one for the feedback. Record what was hard.

Finish by replying with one line: DONE.

# 6. When to Compile: Caches, Load-Time Generation and Tiers

A compiler's output can be produced at four different moments, and the choice determines who waits and for how long. This article sets out those moments, states what the project does today, and works through the designs that would remove the compile from the path of an ordinary boot. By the end you should be able to list what a cache key for compiled code must contain and why, explain what is gained and lost by shipping a checked intermediate form instead of machine code, compute the break-even point for native compilation from the project's measurements, and say when mixing interpreted and native code in one application is worth its complexity.

The article uses the terms *reactor*, *engine* and *turn* from Article 1 and the measurements of Article 2.

## 6.1 Four moments

| Moment | Where | How often | Who waits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Build time | Workstation, when the firmware is built | Once per release | Nobody on the device |
| Install time | Device, when a source file changes | Once per edit | The person who edited |
| Load time | Device, when a world starts | Every boot | Every user, every boot |
| Run time | Device, while the program runs | When code proves to be hot | The running program, briefly |

The two compilers of this project currently sit in different rows. CJI compiles at **install time**: the result is stored on the device's file system and reused on later boots. The typed compiler compiles at **load time**: Files, Agenda and Editor are compiled from source on every boot. For Editor that is 1.99 seconds for WebAssembly or 3.14 seconds for native code, paid each time the device starts, to produce output identical to the previous boot's.

The reason is historical. Compiling from source on the device was the property the project set out to demonstrate, and compiling at boot demonstrates it on every run. Now that it has been demonstrated, the cost can be moved.

## 6.2 What on-device compilation buys and costs

Before optimizing the moment of compilation, it is worth stating why the device compiles at all. A user could, in principle, be given only precompiled modules.

Three things are gained. A program edited on the handheld can be run on the handheld, with no workstation. One source text serves two engines, since the same typed source produces a WebAssembly module or an RV32 module. A new firmware release with a changed reactor does not strand previously installed applications, because they can be recompiled against it.

Three things are paid. The compiler occupies flash: 43 kB of JavaScript source for the typed compiler, against about 660 kB for the CJI tool. It occupies memory while it runs: a peak of 1.5 MB for Editor's WebAssembly build and 2.5 MB for its native build. It must be trusted: an error in a compiler that runs on the device is an error in every program it produces, a point Article 7 develops.

## 6.3 A cache keyed by content

The direct remedy for compiling at every boot is to keep the result. A **cache** maps a key to a stored output. The entire difficulty lies in choosing the key so that a stored output is returned only when a fresh compile would have produced exactly the same bytes.

The output of the typed compiler is a function of five inputs, and the key must cover all of them.

| Input | Why it affects the output |
| --- | --- |
| The application's source text | It is what is compiled |
| The compiler's own source | A changed compiler emits different code for the same source |
| The reactor | The compiled code is copied into it and calls into it at fixed positions |
| The target engine | WebAssembly and RV32 outputs differ |
| The table of functions the reactor offers | Calls are bound by position in that table |

The standard construction is to compute a cryptographic hash of each input and use the combination as the key. Two builds with the same key had the same inputs and therefore the same output. If any input changes, the key changes, the lookup misses, and the compiler runs. No input needs a version number maintained by hand.

This design has a precise description in the literature on build systems. Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones separate a build system into a *scheduler*, which decides the order of work, and a *rebuilder*, which decides whether a piece of work must be redone [Mokhov et al. 2018]. A record of input hashes together with the output's hash is what they call a verifying trace; storing the output itself under that record makes it a constructive trace, from which the output can be restored without rebuilding. The cache proposed here is a constructive trace with one entry per application and engine.

The project has already built this once. The CJI installer stores the compiled module and the source in one of two slots on the file system and writes a small record to non-volatile storage. The record holds the hash of the source, the hash of the compiled module, and the identity of the firmware build. At boot the bytes are checked against the record, and a changed firmware identity discards the cached module. The measured effect is the one to expect for the typed compiler: a cold recompile of a small test program took 7,028 ms, and reuse of the stored module took about 1,450 ms at boot.

Two engineering details from that implementation carry over.

- **Write order.** The module and the source are written to storage first, and the record is updated last. A power loss in between leaves the old record pointing at the old, intact module.
- **Verification on read.** The stored module's hash is recomputed at boot. A damaged module is detected and rebuilt; in the project's test this took 7,047 ms and required no user action.

### A finer grain: one entry per function

Article 4 established that the typed compiler compiles each function from its own text and the declarations of what it calls. That property permits a cache with one entry per *function*. The key for a function is the hash of its text together with the hashes of the signatures and record layouts it mentions. After an edit to one function, only that function misses.

Editor has 120 functions and compiles in about two seconds, so the average function costs under 20 ms on the device. An edit-and-run cycle would then cost one function's compile plus a link step. The link step exists because functions call each other by index and the indices must be assigned consistently; in WebAssembly this is a renumbering of call operands, and it is the same kind of patching the reactor linker already performs. This design was listed in the project's device-language document and not built. It follows from local checking with no further analysis.

## 6.4 Shipping a checked intermediate form

A second design stores neither source nor machine code. It stores an intermediate form that has already been parsed and checked, and generates machine code from it when the program is loaded.

The reference work is **slim binaries**. Franz and Kistler distributed programs for the Oberon system as a compact encoding of the program's syntax tree, and the loader generated native code for whatever processor it ran on [Franz & Kistler 1997]. The motivation was portability: one file ran on several processor families. Their report on speed is careful and worth repeating exactly. Because the encoding was much smaller than native code, the time saved reading it from disk "can almost compensate for the extra time" of generating code; on the fastest machine they measured, loading a suite of applications from slim binaries took about two seconds, almost twice the time of loading native binaries, which they judged competitive. Franz's dissertation, on a different processor, reported that loading with code generation required "little more time than the input of equivalent native code" [Franz 1994].

On this device WebAssembly plays the role of the slim binary. It is target-independent, it is compact (88 kB for Editor against 240 kB of native module), and it can be checked for well-formedness in one forward pass. The designers of WebAssembly state that its structured control flow allows code "to be validated in a single pass, compiled in a single pass, or even transformed to an SSA-form intermediate form in a single pass" [Haas et al. 2017].

Three storage choices follow, and the measurements of Article 2 let us compare them for the native Editor.

| What is stored | Work at each boot | Approximate boot cost on the device | Flash used |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Source only (today) | Tokenize, parse, check, emit, lower, link | 3.1 s | 71 kB |
| Checked WebAssembly | Lower and link only | about 1.2 s | 88 kB |
| Native module | Verify the hash and load | about 0.01 s to load, plus hashing | 240 kB |

The middle row is the slim-binary design: it removes the frontend, which Experiment 3 found to be about 58 percent of the native compile path, and keeps the stored form portable across engines. The third row is the cache of section 6.3. Flash is not the scarce resource here, since the firmware partition is 8 MiB and holds about 4.4 MB, so the third row is the better choice for boot time. The second remains useful as the form in which an application is *distributed*, because a module in that form can be given to either engine.

What is lost by storing a compiled form of any kind is exactly one thing: the stored form can become stale. That is the problem the content key of section 6.3 solves.

### Native modules and virtual machines on small devices

The comparison between loading native code and interpreting compact code has been measured before on machines much smaller than this one. Dunkels and colleagues built a loader for standard ELF object files in the Contiki operating system for sensor nodes and compared it with an application-specific virtual machine and a Java virtual machine [Dunkels et al. 2006]. Native code was cheaper to execute and more expensive to transmit and link, so each program had a break-even point. For their object-tracking program, interpretation became more expensive than native loading only after about 40,000 to 80,000 iterations. Their conclusion was that the right choice depends on how often code is replaced relative to how much it runs, and that a system can reasonably offer both.

The Maté virtual machine took the opposite extreme deliberately. It fitted in 1 kB of RAM and 16 kB of program memory, and its programs were capsules of at most 24 one-byte instructions, small enough to fit in one radio packet [Levis & Culler 2002]. Its authors argued that for programs replaced often, the energy saved by shipping tiny programs outweighs the energy spent interpreting them. The same reasoning applies on the handheld to code that changes with every keystroke of an edit session, and it is why QuickJS and WebAssembly remain the right engines for code under development.

## 6.5 Break-even arithmetic

The textbook states the constraint on any compiler that runs at the user's expense: "the system must recoup compile time through improved running time" [Cooper & Torczon 2023, §1.4]. The project's numbers allow the calculation.

For Editor, producing native code instead of WebAssembly costs 3.14 − 1.99 = 1.15 seconds more at compile time. It saves 8.8 − 1.6 = 7.2 ms of processor time per turn. The extra compile is repaid after 1.15 s / 7.2 ms ≈ 160 turns. If the compile happens at every boot, native code is a loss in any session shorter than 160 key presses. If the compile happens once per change of the source, it is repaid within the first few minutes of use and is free afterwards. Caching changes the answer to the question "should this application be native".

For CJI the same calculation was made in the project's device-language study. Compiling Files with CJI took 140.6 seconds in the best case, against 0.082 seconds to register the JavaScript version with QuickJS. If native code saved one millisecond on every call into the application, the compile would be repaid after about 140,000 calls.

## 6.6 Tiers and mixed mode

A **tiered** system runs code in a cheap form first and produces a better form only for the parts that are executed often. Article 3 described Self's two compilers. The Smalltalk-80 system of Deutsch and Schiffman is the earlier instance: it translated a method from compact virtual-machine code to native code the first time the method ran, cached the native code, and discarded it when memory was short, regenerating it on demand. Their native code took about five times the space of the virtual-machine code [Deutsch & Schiffman 1984]. The textbook calls the discard policy throw-away code generation and gives the general range as a factor of two to five [Cooper & Torczon 2023, chapter 14].

This project's measured ratio is inside that range: 4.76 bytes of RV32 per byte of WebAssembly function body for Editor. The size has a concrete consequence, which is the reason mixed mode comes up at all. Each world has a memory limit, 768 KiB for Editor, and the native Editor uses 710 KiB of it where the WebAssembly Editor uses 528 KiB. The binding resource is the world's memory limit, and the native version is close to it.

**Mixed mode** would compile only the hot functions of an application to native code and leave the rest as WebAssembly. It would buy most of the speed for a fraction of the size. It costs three things: a way to find the hot functions, which means counters and a trigger [Cooper & Torczon 2023, §14.2]; a calling path between the interpreter and native code in both directions; and the acceptance of unconfined native code inside an otherwise confined world.

The recommendation of this issue is not to build mixed mode now. Article 5 predicts that a better backend brings native code to between 1.4 and 1.8 times the size of the WebAssembly, at which point the whole application fits comfortably as native code and the selection machinery is unnecessary. Mixed mode remains the fallback if that prediction fails.

## 6.7 Doing the work before the device boots

The cheapest compile is the one done on the workstation. Two systems for microcontrollers show how far this can be taken.

The Moddable SDK's **preload** feature executes the top-level code of JavaScript modules during the build, on the build machine, and stores the resulting objects in flash, so that the device starts with those modules already initialized and their data out of RAM. MicroPython can likewise store precompiled bytecode, and since 2019 precompiled native code, in files produced on a workstation.

The project has one instance of this idea already, applied at boot instead of at build: the JavaScript prelude, which every QuickJS world used to compile from source, is now compiled once per boot and the result shared, which reduced that work from 627 ms to 198 ms.

For the typed applications bundled with the firmware, the same compiler can run under Node during the firmware build and place its output in the image. The compiler is deterministic, and the harness built for Experiment 3 already produces a module of exactly the size the device produces. A bundled application would then start from a prebuilt module whose key is checked at boot, and the on-device compiler would run only for source that was edited on the device.

## 6.8 A combined design

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B["World starts"] --> K["Compute key: source, compiler, reactor, engine, import table"]
    K --> H{"Stored module with this key?"}
    H -->|"yes"| V["Verify module hash"] --> L["Load"]
    H -->|"no"| C["Compile on the device"] --> S["Store module, then record"] --> L
    F["Firmware build on workstation"] -.->|"prebuilt modules and keys for bundled apps"| H
```

With this design an unedited application costs a hash check and a load at boot. An edited application costs one compile, once. The on-device compiler remains fully exercised, because every edit runs it.

## 6.9 Key points

- The typed compiler runs at every boot and produces the same output each time. Editor pays 2.0 to 3.1 seconds for this.
- A cache key must cover every input that affects the output: source, compiler, reactor, engine and the reactor's function table. Hashing the inputs makes this automatic.
- Store the output first and the record last, and verify the output's hash when reading.
- WebAssembly can serve as a checked, portable distribution form from which native code is generated at load, as slim binaries did. Storing the native module is faster at boot when flash is available, as it is here.
- With compilation at every boot, native Editor repays its extra compile time after about 160 turns. With caching it is repaid once.
- Mixed mode is a response to native code size. A better backend makes it unnecessary.

## 6.10 Check your understanding

1. The typed compiler's source file is changed in a firmware update, and the application's source is unchanged. Should a cached module be reused? Explain using the list of inputs in section 6.3.
2. Why is the record written after the module, and what does the device find after a power loss between the two writes?
3. Using the figures in section 6.5, compute how many turns are needed to repay the extra cost of native compilation for Editor, and state how caching changes the conclusion.
4. Franz and Kistler reported that loading from slim binaries took almost twice as long as loading native binaries on their fastest machine. Give the reason they still considered the design worthwhile, and name the form that plays the slim binary's role on the handheld.
5. Which resource limit makes native code size a concern for Editor, and what are the two memory figures that show it?
6. An edit changes the body of one function out of 120 and no signature. With a per-function cache, what is recompiled and what additional step is still required?

## References

- [Cooper & Torczon 2023] K. D. Cooper, L. Torczon. *Engineering a Compiler*, 3rd edition. Morgan Kaufmann, 2023. §1.4, chapter 14.
- [Deutsch & Schiffman 1984] L. P. Deutsch, A. M. Schiffman. "Efficient implementation of the Smalltalk-80 system." *POPL*, 1984.
- [Dunkels et al. 2006] A. Dunkels, N. Finne, J. Eriksson, T. Voigt. "Run-time dynamic linking for reprogramming wireless sensor networks." *SenSys*, 2006.
- [Franz 1994] M. Franz. "Code-generation on-the-fly: a key to portable software." Doctoral dissertation, ETH Zürich, 1994.
- [Franz & Kistler 1997] M. Franz, T. Kistler. "Slim binaries." *Communications of the ACM* 40(12), 1997. Quotations are from the technical-report version, UC Irvine ICS TR 96-24, 1996.
- [Haas et al. 2017] A. Haas, A. Rossberg, D. L. Schuff, B. L. Titzer, M. Holman, D. Gohman, L. Wagner, A. Zakai, J. F. Bastien. "Bringing the web up to speed with WebAssembly." *PLDI*, 2017.
- [Levis & Culler 2002] P. Levis, D. Culler. "Maté: a tiny virtual machine for sensor networks." *ASPLOS*, 2002.
- [Mokhov et al. 2018] A. Mokhov, N. Mitchell, S. Peyton Jones. "Build systems à la carte." *ICFP*, 2018.
- Moddable SDK documentation, "Using XS Preload to Optimize Applications".
- MicroPython documentation, "Maximising MicroPython speed".

# Investigation entry

Use this full format for substantive implementation, design, debugging, or an explicit detailed-diary request. Begin each step with 1–2 prose paragraphs. The prompt is verbatim once, then referenced. Preserve exact failures, not invented or reconstructed diagnostics.

```markdown
## Step N: Descriptive title

One or two short paragraphs explaining intent, change and outcome.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Actual authored request" (or: see Step N)
**Assistant interpretation:** What is being requested.
**Inferred user intent:** Intended outcome and reason.
**Commit (code):** hash — "message" (when available)

### What I did
- Concrete files, symbols and commands.

### Why
- Rationale and considered alternatives.

### What worked
- Evidence-backed outcomes.

### What didn't work
- Exact command, diagnostic, scope and recovery; or no failures observed.

### What I learned
- Corrected assumptions and constraints.

### What was tricky to build
- Underlying cause, symptoms and exact solution, including ordering/lifetime boundaries.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- Review-critical correctness, concurrency, security or performance questions.

### What should be done in the future
- Follow-ups implied by this step; N/A if none.

### Code review instructions
- Starting files/symbols and validation commands.

### Technical details
- Concrete contracts, snippets, limits and references.
```

Do not add compatibility shims unless required. Record behavior changes and update tests/docs. A passing test alone does not prove all user requirements are satisfied.

# Answers to "Check your understanding"

## 1. Compiler changed in a firmware update, application source unchanged

No, the cached module should not be reused. Section 6.3 lists five inputs the key must cover, and "the compiler's own source" is one of them, because a changed compiler emits different code for the same source. If the key is a hash of all five inputs, then changing the compiler source changes the key, the lookup misses, and the compiler runs again. The application's source being unchanged is irrelevant, since only the whole key has to match.

Working: old key = H(source, compiler_v1, reactor, engine, import_table); new key = H(source, compiler_v2, reactor, engine, import_table); the two keys differ because compiler_v1 ≠ compiler_v2, so the lookup misses.

Confidence: 5

## 2. Why the record is written last, and what a power loss leaves

The module and the source are written to storage first; only after they are safely there is the small record (hashes plus firmware identity) updated. The record is the thing that makes stored data "valid", so writing it last means it never points at bytes that were not yet written. After a power loss between the two writes the old record survives, and it still points at the old module, which was never overwritten and is therefore intact and still verifiable. So the device boots into the last consistent state rather than into a half-written one.

Confidence: 5

## 3. Break-even turns for native Editor, and the effect of caching

Extra compile cost: 3.14 s (native) − 1.99 s (WebAssembly) = 1.15 s = 1150 ms. Saving per turn: 8.8 ms − 1.6 ms = 7.2 ms. Turns to repay = 1150 / 7.2 = 159.7, so about 160 turns. If the compile happens at every boot, any session shorter than 160 key presses is a net loss for native code. With caching the 1.15 s is paid once per change of the source rather than once per boot, so the balance turns positive within the first few minutes of use and stays positive for every later boot.

Confidence: 5

## 4. Why slim binaries were still worthwhile, and WebAssembly's role

The slim-binary encoding was much smaller than native code, so less time was spent reading the file from disk, and that saving "can almost compensate for the extra time" spent generating code. On their fastest machine the load took about two seconds, almost twice the native load time, and they judged that competitive — the gain is portability, since one file then runs on several processor families. They also measured that on a different processor the load plus code generation took "little more time" than reading equivalent native code. On the handheld, WebAssembly plays the slim binary's role: it is the compact, target-independent, checked form from which native code is generated at load (88 kB for Editor against 240 kB of native module).

Confidence: 4

## 5. Which resource limit makes native size a concern

The binding resource is each world's memory limit, not flash. Editor's world has a limit of 768 KiB, the native Editor uses 710 KiB of it, and the WebAssembly Editor uses only 528 KiB. So native Editor sits close to the ceiling while the WebAssembly version has headroom, which is why compiling everything natively is risky and why mixed mode is discussed as a fallback. Flash is not scarce: the firmware partition is 8 MiB and holds about 4.4 MB.

Confidence: 5

## 6. One edited function body, no signature change, per-function cache

Only that one function misses the cache, so only its text is recompiled; at Editor's average of under 20 ms per function that is the whole compile cost. Nothing else is recompiled, because the other functions' keys are hashes of their own text plus the signatures and record layouts they mention, and none of those changed. A link step is still required, because functions call each other by index and the indices must be assigned consistently; in WebAssembly this is a renumbering of call operands, the same kind of patching the reactor linker already does. So the cycle is one function's compile plus a link, not a full build.

Confidence: 4

# Feedback on "6. When to Compile: Caches, Load-Time Generation and Tiers"

I am a student reader with no access to Articles 1–5 or 7, to Article 2's measurements, or to the
project's source. I read the article as a standalone text, which is how I judged it.

## Passages I had to read twice

1. "Because the encoding was much smaller than native code, the time saved reading it from disk 'can almost compensate for the extra time' of generating code; on the fastest machine they measured, loading a suite of applications from slim binaries took about two seconds, almost twice the time of loading native binaries, which they judged competitive."

I could not reconcile the three halves of this sentence. If loading takes almost twice as long as
native, the disk saving did *not* compensate on that machine; "almost compensate" is doing a lot of
work. Then "which they judged competitive" attaches to a number I cannot evaluate — twice the load
time of what baseline, against what benefit? The paragraph needs to say plainly: on machine A the
load is 2× native, this is still competitive because X, and on machine B it is ~1×.

2. "The middle row is the slim-binary design: it removes the frontend, which Experiment 3 found to be about 58 percent of the native compile path, and keeps the stored form portable across engines."

I had to re-read this against the table because the arithmetic does not land. 58 percent of 3.14 s
removed leaves about 1.32 s, but the table says "about 1.2 s". The difference is small, but for a
reader trying to check the article's own numbers the missing 0.1 s is a distraction. Say "about
1.3 s" or explain what else the 1.2 s excludes.

3. "The record holds the hash of the source, the hash of the compiled module, and the identity of the firmware build. At boot the bytes are checked against the record, and a changed firmware identity discards the cached module."

Here the CJI record holds only *three* things, while 6.3 just argued the key must cover *five*
inputs. Is the firmware identity a stand-in for (compiler, reactor, import table)? If so, say so,
because otherwise the two paragraphs contradict each other and the reader is left unsure which
list is the real key.

4. "This project's measured ratio is inside that range: 4.76 bytes of RV32 per byte of WebAssembly function body for Editor. ... the native Editor uses 710 KiB of it where the WebAssembly Editor uses 528 KiB."

I had to work out why 4.76 does not match 240 kB / 88 kB ≈ 2.7. The answer seems to be that 4.76 is
per byte of *function body* while the module sizes include headers and data. That distinction is
never stated and it makes two nearby numbers look inconsistent.

## Terms used before they were explained, or never explained

- **reactor** — used in the introduction as if known ("the terms *reactor*, *engine* and *turn* from Article 1"); never defined here.
- **engine** — same; I inferred "WebAssembly or RV32" from the table, but only by guessing.
- **turn** — same; only reconstructable via "key presses" in 6.5.
- **CJI** — introduced cold in 6.1 ("CJI compiles at install time"); never expanded, never said what it is or why it has two compilers.
- **typed compiler** — contrasted with CJI throughout; what "typed" means is never stated.
- **world** — "when a world starts", "each world has a memory limit"; never defined.
- **lower / lowering** — appears in the 6.4 table ("emit, lower, link", "Lower and link only") with no explanation of what lowering is.
- **link / link step** — used in 6.3 and 6.4; the reader is told indices must be assigned, but "link" as a stage name arrives unannounced.
- **verifying trace / constructive trace** — defined by contrast in one sentence, but "trace" alone is never given a plain-language gloss.
- **frontend** — "the frontend" in 6.4; presumably tokenize+parse+check, but not said.
- **prelude** — "the JavaScript prelude"; a JavaScript reader can guess, a general reader cannot.
- **confined world / unconfined native code** — security/isolation vocabulary used once, in passing, with no explanation.
- **QuickJS** — named as an engine without introduction.
- **capsule** — Maté's unit; explained by its size, not by what it is.
- **non-volatile storage** — technical but standard; listed only because the article is careful elsewhere.
- **SSA-form** — appears inside a quotation, unexplained.

## Claims I could not verify from the article itself

1. **"a peak of 1.5 MB for Editor's WebAssembly build and 2.5 MB for its native build"** and **"43 kB of JavaScript source for the typed compiler, against about 660 kB for the CJI tool"** — no measuring method, no pointer to the experiment that produced them. Article 2 is credited for "the measurements" in general, but not for these.

2. **"Experiment 3 found to be about 58 percent of the native compile path"** — the experiment is never described here: what it timed, on what device, with what variance. I am asked to accept a percentage and then do arithmetic with it.

3. **"It saves 8.8 − 1.6 = 7.2 ms of processor time per turn"** — the two source numbers appear nowhere else in the article. Question 3 of the quiz depends on them, so they should carry a citation or a one-line derivation.

4. **"about 0.01 s to load, plus hashing"** — the phrase "plus hashing" hides an unknown. Hashing 240 kB may well dominate 10 ms, and that would change the comparison in the table's favour of the middle row. No figure is given.

5. **"loading with code generation required 'little more time than the input of equivalent native code' [Franz 1994]"** — quoted without the machine, benchmark or units, so it cannot be weighed against the 2 s figure from the 1997 report.

6. **"The compiler is deterministic, and the harness built for Experiment 3 already produces a module of exactly the size the device produces."** — determinism is exactly what the whole cache design rests on, and it is asserted in half a sentence. One line on *how* it is known (no timestamps, no hash-order iteration, stable index assignment) would be worth more than the harness aside.

7. **"the harness … produces a module of exactly the size the device produces"** — "exactly the size" is a strange proxy for "exactly the same bytes", which is what the cache needs. If only size is known to match, the cache argument is weaker than claimed.

8. **"reuse of the stored module took about 1,450 ms at boot"** — as a "measured effect … the one to expect for the typed compiler" this is compared with 7,028 ms cold, which is a 4.8× gain, but the article also predicts loading a native module is ~0.01 s. Why does reuse still cost 1.45 s? Is it verification, or hashing, or something else? Unresolved.

9. **"4.76 bytes of RV32 per byte of WebAssembly function body"** — as noted above, this contradicts the module-size ratio of about 2.7 and the article never reconciles the two.

10. **"Article 5 predicts that a better backend brings native code to between 1.4 and 1.8 times the size of the WebAssembly"** — a prediction used to justify not building mixed mode; nothing here lets me judge its basis.

## Section scores

- **6.1 Four moments — 5.** The table is the clearest thing in the article; who waits, and how often, is exactly the right frame, and the per-boot cost of Editor is stated immediately.
- **6.2 What on-device compilation buys and costs — 4.** Three gains and three costs in a clean pattern; only the unexplained 660 kB CJI figure and the undefined "CJI"/"typed" keep it from 5.
- **6.3 A cache keyed by content — 4.** The five-input table and the write-order/verify-on-read rules are genuinely teachable; the CJI record's three fields versus the five-input key is the contradiction I had to resolve myself.
- **6.4 Shipping a checked intermediate form — 3.** The idea is clear and the three-row table is good, but the slim-binary quotation is muddled, the 58 percent / 1.2 s arithmetic does not close, and the 4.76-versus-2.7 size ratio is left dangling.
- **6.5 Break-even arithmetic — 4.** The Editor calculation is fully worked and easy to follow; the 8.8 ms and 1.6 ms inputs appear from nowhere, and the CJI figure (140.6 s vs 0.082 s) is asserted rather than derived in the text.
- **6.6 Tiers and mixed mode — 4.** Smalltalk-80 as the earlier instance, throw-away code generation, and the three costs of mixed mode are all well put; "confined world" is jargon dropped without support.
- **6.7 Doing the work before the device boots — 3.** The examples (Moddable preload, MicroPython, the prelude going from 627 ms to 198 ms) are concrete, but the section is short and ends by asserting the compiler is deterministic without evidence.
- **6.8 A combined design — 5.** The diagram says in ten words what the rest of the article argued; the dotted build-time arrow into the "stored module?" test is the right picture.
- **6.9 Key points — 5.** Accurate and traceable back to the sections, which is more than most summaries achieve.
- **6.10 Check your understanding — 4.** Five of six questions are answerable from the text alone; question 4 asks about a paragraph I found internally confusing, so it tests the muddle as much as the idea.

## Questions that the article did not let me answer

None of the six was unanswerable, which is a point in the article's favour. Two needed repair work:

- **Question 4** is answerable only if I accept "can almost compensate" at face value and skip the tension with "almost twice as long". The article gives the reason (smaller file, portability) but never resolves why a 2× load penalty is called competitive, so my answer is a restatement rather than an explanation.
- **Question 3** is fully answerable only because the article supplies 8.8 ms and 1.6 ms in 6.5. Those two numbers are otherwise unsupported, so the arithmetic I performed is really the article's arithmetic handed to me, not a check of it.
- **Question 6** is answerable but I could not say *why* the renumbering is cheap, or how large the link step is relative to the 20 ms compile. The article says the link "is the same kind of patching the reactor linker already performs" without a cost.

## One thing to add and one thing to cut

**Add:** a two-sentence definition box, early in 6.1, for the vocabulary the article inherits —
reactor, engine, turn, world, CJI versus the typed compiler, and what "lower" and "link" mean as
stages. The article is well organised and its tables are excellent, but it repeatedly asks the
reader to hold a model built in Articles 1 and 2 that is never handed over. Six or seven lines,
placed once, would remove most of the double readings listed above.

**Cut:** the long slim-binary quotation paragraph in 6.4 as it currently stands. It stacks three
hedged numbers (a disk saving that "can almost compensate", two seconds versus native, "little more
time" on a different processor) into one sentence-chain, and a reader cannot extract a clean claim
from it. One sentence — "Franz and Kistler accepted a load time up to about twice native because the
file was portable and much smaller" — carries everything the section needs, and frees the space for
the definition box above.

# Investigation entry: Student read of article 6, "When to Compile"

Three steps: reading the article, answering the quiz, writing the feedback. The files produced are
`answers.md` and `feedback.md` in this directory.

## Step 1: Reading the article

I read `TASK.md` first, then `article.md` straight through without stopping, then went back over
6.3, 6.4 and 6.5 with the tables side by side, because those are the sections where the numbers
have to agree with each other. My aim was to read as an ordinary student would: no access to
Articles 1–5 or 7, no access to Article 2's measurements, and no web lookups.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Read TASK.md and carry out every step in order."
**Assistant interpretation:** Act as the student reader described in `TASK.md`: read the article, answer its quiz into `answers.md`, write structured criticism into `feedback.md`, and keep this diary.
**Inferred user intent:** The editor wants to know where the teaching article fails before publication, and specifically wants the failure modes named by passage, not a general verdict.
**Commit (code):** N/A — no code changes in this session.

### What I did
- Read `TASK.md`, `diary-format.md`, then the full `article.md` (sections 6.1–6.10 plus references).
- Re-read 6.1, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5, 6.6 in a second pass with the four tables (6.1 moments, 6.2 none, 6.3 inputs, 6.4 storage choices) next to each other.
- Jotted the arithmetic checks by hand: 3.14 − 1.99 = 1.15 s; 1.15 / 0.0072 ≈ 160 turns; 240/88 ≈ 2.7 versus the stated 4.76; 0.58 × 3.14 ≈ 1.82 s removed, leaving ≈1.32 s versus the stated "about 1.2 s"; 140.6 − 0.082 s ≈ 140,500 ms of calls.

### Why
- A single fast pass would have hidden the internal inconsistencies, which only show up when the numbers in prose are compared with the numbers in tables.
- I deliberately did not reconstruct the missing definitions from general knowledge of compilers, because the point of the test is whether the article teaches them.

### What worked
- The structure is genuinely navigable: every section states its claim up front, and the key-points list in 6.9 maps back to the sections without contradiction.
- The 6.4 "what is stored / work at each boot / cost / flash" table and the 6.8 mermaid diagram are the two places where I understood the design without needing anything else.
- The break-even section 6.5 is the only place where I could check the article's arithmetic end to end and have it come out right.

### What didn't work
- Reading section 6.4's slim-binary paragraph, I could not decide whether the design was "as fast as native" or "twice as slow but fine". No amount of re-reading resolved it; I recorded it as a double-read in `feedback.md`.
- The 4.76-per-byte-of-function-body figure versus the 240 kB / 88 kB module sizes looked like an error until I guessed the scope difference. My guess is not stated in the article, so it stays a guess.

### What I learned
- The article's weakest point is not its argument but its inherited vocabulary. Reactor, engine, turn, world, CJI, lower, link and frontend are all load-bearing and all undefined here.
- Its strongest point is that every design choice is attached to a measured consequence, so I could score the sections on clarity rather than on agreement.

### What was tricky to build
- Question 4 of the quiz is the hard case: I could answer it, but only by paraphrasing a paragraph I had just flagged as unclear. I marked that in the feedback rather than pretending the section was fine.
- Question 3 depends on 8.8 ms and 1.6 ms, which appear nowhere else in the article. Answering it is therefore not really a check of the text, and I said so.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- Whether the 4.76 ratio and the 88 kB / 240 kB module sizes are meant to be reconcilable — someone with access to Article 2 can settle this in a minute.
- Whether the CJI record's three fields really are equivalent to the five-input key of 6.3, or whether that paragraph needs rewriting.

### What should be done in the future
- If the article is revised, re-run this student read against the revised text, especially quiz question 4, to check that the slim-binary paragraph has become answerable in one reading.

### Code review instructions
- No code. Read `answers.md` first, then `feedback.md`; every criticism in the latter quotes the passage it refers to, so it can be checked against `article.md` by search.

### Technical details
- Files read: `TASK.md`, `diary-format.md`, `article.md`. Files written: `answers.md`, `feedback.md`, `diary.md`.
- Quiz answered: 6 questions, each 2–6 sentences with a `Confidence: N` line.
- Confidence given: 5 on questions 1, 2, 3, 5; 4 on questions 4 and 6.

## Step 2: Answering the quiz

I answered the six questions in `answers.md`, numbered 1–6 as the article numbers them, keeping each
to two to six sentences and showing the arithmetic where a question asked for it. I wrote the
answers in my own words rather than copying sentences out of the article, except where the article's
own phrasing is the claim being tested.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** see Step 1
**Assistant interpretation:** Produce `answers.md` with one numbered answer per quiz question and a `Confidence: N` line under each.
**Inferred user intent:** The editor wants to see not only whether the questions can be answered but how sure a reader feels, since low confidence on an answerable question is itself a signal of unclear writing.
**Commit (code):** N/A.

### What I did
- Wrote six answers, each with a short working line where the question was computational (questions 1, 3, 6).
- Assigned confidence: 5 for 1, 2, 3, 5; 4 for 4 and 6.

### Why
- Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q5 have their answers stated in the text almost directly, so anything below 5 would have been dishonest.
- Q4 got 4 because the paragraph it rests on is self-tensioned; Q6 got 4 because the article says the link step exists and what it does, but not what it costs, so I could not judge whether "one function's compile plus a link" is actually cheap.

### What worked
- The five-input table in 6.3 made Q1 mechanical: change one input, the key changes.
- The write-order bullet in 6.3 made Q2 answerable in one pass.
- Q3's numbers were all present in 6.5 and the arithmetic reproduced exactly (159.7 ≈ 160).

### What didn't work
- For Q6 I initially wrote that only the function is recompiled, which is incomplete: the link step is required because indices shift. Re-reading 6.3's "one entry per function" subsection corrected this.
- For Q4 my first draft repeated the phrase "can almost compensate" without explaining it, which is exactly the failure the article commits; I rewrote it to state the intended reason (smaller file, portability) and to note the tension.

### What I learned
- Answering a quiz is a much sharper test of an article than reading it: three of my first drafts turned out to be restatements of unclear sentences rather than explanations.
- Confidence numbers are a useful forcing device — writing "5" made me go back and confirm the text actually said it.

### What was tricky to build
- Q3 asks specifically how *caching* changes the conclusion, which requires combining 6.5's arithmetic with 6.3's design. The article never states that combined conclusion in one place, so I had to assemble it from "repaid within the first few minutes of use" plus "the answer to 'should this application be native' changes".

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- My Q4 answer is the one I would want checked against the original Franz & Kistler report; I can only report what this article quotes.

### What should be done in the future
- N/A.

### Code review instructions
- Check `answers.md` against sections 6.3, 6.4, 6.5 and 6.6 of `article.md`; the arithmetic in Q3 should reproduce at 1.15 s / 7.2 ms.

### Technical details
- Q3 working: 3.14 − 1.99 = 1.15 s; 8.8 − 1.6 = 7.2 ms; 1150 / 7.2 = 159.7 → about 160 turns.
- Q1 working: key = H(source, compiler source, reactor, engine, import table); compiler source changes, so the key changes.

## Step 3: Writing the feedback

I wrote `feedback.md` in the six sections `TASK.md` asks for, quoting each passage I criticised so the
editor can find it. The aim was to be specific enough to act on: not "section 6.4 is unclear" but
"this sentence stacks three hedged numbers and here is why I could not extract a claim from it".

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** see Step 1
**Assistant interpretation:** Produce `feedback.md` with the six required sections: double-read passages, undefined terms, unverifiable claims, per-section scores, unanswerable quiz questions, and one addition plus one cut.
**Inferred user intent:** Give the editor an actionable list of failures, ordered by where to look, plus a prioritised suggestion for what to change.
**Commit (code):** N/A.

### What I did
- Collected four passages I read twice, with the specific reason each time.
- Listed sixteen terms used before definition or never defined, one line each.
- Listed ten claims I could not verify from the article alone, quote plus missing evidence.
- Scored all ten numbered sections 1–5 with a one-sentence reason: 6.1 = 5, 6.2 = 4, 6.3 = 4, 6.4 = 3, 6.5 = 4, 6.6 = 4, 6.7 = 3, 6.8 = 5, 6.9 = 5, 6.10 = 4.
- Answered the "questions the article did not let me answer" section honestly: none of the six was strictly unanswerable, but Q4 and Q3 needed repair work, and Q6 could be answered without being able to judge the cost.

### Why
- I scored 6.4 and 6.7 lowest because those are the two places where I had to guess at missing information (the 1.2 s figure, the determinism claim) rather than merely look something up in an earlier section.
- I chose "add a definition box" as the addition because the undefined-terms list is by far the longest section of my feedback; one fix pays off across the whole article.
- I chose the slim-binary paragraph as the cut because it is both the least clear passage and the one that quiz question 4 depends on.

### What worked
- Quoting each passage made the criticism checkable; I could re-verify every complaint against the file before writing it down.
- The section scores came out spread (3 to 5) rather than uniform, which suggests they are measuring something real.

### What didn't work
- The instruction "questions that the article did not let me answer" presupposed some failure; in fact all six were answerable. I could have simply written "none" but judged that naming the two weak cases was more useful than a one-word answer, so I did both.

### What I learned
- The article's problems cluster: inheritance of vocabulary from earlier articles, and numbers quoted without their source. Almost every item in my list falls into one of those two buckets.
- A table can be clear while the prose beside it is not — 6.4 is the example.

### What was tricky to build
- Distinguishing "I could not verify this" from "I disagree with this". Several claims (the 1.4–1.8× backend prediction, the 58 percent frontend share) are plausible but unsupported *here*; I recorded them as missing evidence rather than as errors.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- My score of 3 for 6.4 is the one most likely to be contested, since the section's central idea is well explained and only its supporting paragraph fails.

### What should be done in the future
- If the editor accepts the definition-box suggestion, the sixteen-term list is the specification for what it must contain.

### Code review instructions
- Read `feedback.md` sections in order; each quoted passage can be located in `article.md` by search.

### Technical details
- Section scores: 6.1 = 5, 6.2 = 4, 6.3 = 4, 6.4 = 3, 6.5 = 4, 6.6 = 4, 6.7 = 3, 6.8 = 5, 6.9 = 5, 6.10 = 4.
- Outputs: `feedback.md` (six sections), `answers.md` (six answers), this diary.

- **`feedback.md`** — the six required sections; notable findings: the slim-binary paragraph is internally self-tensioned (Q4 depends on it), the CJI record's three fields contradict the five-input key of 6.3, 58% of 3.14 s leaves ≈1.32 s not the stated 1.2 s, and 4.76 bytes/function-byte doesn't match 240 kB/88 kB ≈ 2.7. Section scores range 3–5.
- **`diary.md`** — three steps in the `diary-format.md` shape, recording what was hard (answerable-but-repair-needed quiz questions, distinguishing "unverifiable" from "disagree").
